dryRun.title: 0-1 knapsack, capacity 4. Items (weight, value): A (1, 15), B (3, 20), C (4, 30). dp[w] = best value with capacity w
rows: dp[4] = max(15, dp[1] + 20) = 35 (A and B together)
dp[4] = max(35, dp[0] + 30) = 35, so C is not worth it
dryRun.note: Each item is used at most once, so the capacity loop goes downwards: dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - weight] + value) reads the values from before this item was added.

think.q:
const weights = [1, 3, 4], values = [15, 20, 30], W = 4
const dp = new Array(W + 1).fill(0)
for (let i = 0; i < weights.length; i++) {
  for (let w = W; w >= weights[i]; w--) {
    dp[w] = Math.max(dp[w], dp[w - weights[i]] + values[i])
  }
}
console.log(dp[W])
why: Items A and B together weigh 4 and are worth 15 + 20 = 35. Item C alone weighs 4 and is worth only 30.
Taking the item with the best value first (greedy) would pick C and miss the better pair.

think.q:
const weights = [1], values = [15], W = 3
const dp = new Array(W + 1).fill(0)
for (let i = 0; i < weights.length; i++) {
  for (let w = weights[i]; w <= W; w++) {
    dp[w] = Math.max(dp[w], dp[w - weights[i]] + values[i])
  }
}
console.log(dp[W])

There is one item, so the correct answer is 15. What does this print?
why: Going upwards, dp[w - weight] already contains this item, so the same item is added again and again: 15 × 3 = 45.
That is the unbounded knapsack. For 0-1, loop the capacity downwards.

think.q: Why does the capacity loop go from high to low for 0-1 knapsack?
opts: So that each update reads values from before the current item was added, and the item is counted only once
why: When we update a high capacity first, the lower cells it reads have not been changed by this item yet.
The two loops (coins upwards, knapsack downwards) look almost the same and are a favourite interview trap.

think.q: n items and capacity W. What is the time, and why is it called "pseudo-polynomial"?
opts: O(n * W); W is a number, so the cost grows with its value and not with the number of digits
why: The table has n × W cells. If W is a huge number (like 10⁹), the table is too big even though W is "just one number".
With only a 1D array the space is O(W).

think.q: "Can some of these numbers add up exactly to a target?" (subset sum). How does it relate to knapsack?
opts: It is a 0-1 knapsack where the table holds true / false: dp[s] = dp[s] OR dp[s - num]
It is solved with a heap
why: Each number is used at most once, so the sum loop goes downwards, but the cell stores "can I make this sum?" instead of a value.
Partition equal subset sum, and target sum, are the same idea.

try.task: Write knapsack(weights, values, capacity). Each item can be taken at most once. Return the largest total value whose total weight is at most capacity.
try.hint: Use a 1D array dp of length capacity + 1 filled with 0. For each item, loop the capacity from capacity down to the item weight.

checks.verify: assert(knapsack([1], [15], 3) === 15, "expected 15, an item can be used once")

checks.t: zero capacity and an item that is too heavy

checks.verify: const w = Array.from({ length: 100 }, (_, i) => (i % 17) + 3), v = Array.from({ length: 100 }, (_, i) => (i * 7) % 23 + 1); const t0 = Date.now(); const r = knapsack(w, v, 10000); assert(r === v.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) && Date.now() - t0 < 500, "wrong or too slow (capacity is large enough for every item)")

takeaway.key: 0-1 knapsack: dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - weight] + value), with the capacity loop downwards so every item is used once. O(n × W) time, O(W) space. Subset sum is the same with true / false.
mistakes: Looping the capacity upwards (that allows repeats).
Picking items by best value or ratio (greedy fails for 0-1).
Reading dp[w - weight] when the weight is bigger than w.
Using a table that is too big for a huge capacity.

dryRun.title: Stock prices [1, 3, 2, 8, 4, 9], fee 2 per sale. Two states: cash (holding nothing) and hold (holding one share)
dryRun.note: Instead of a table indexed by position only, we keep one value per state. Each day the states move by the allowed actions: cash = max(cash, hold + price - fee) and hold = max(hold, cash - price). The answer is the last cash.

think.q:
const prices = [1, 3, 2, 8, 4, 9], fee = 2
let cash = 0, hold = -prices[0]
for (let i = 1; i < prices.length; i++) {
  const p = prices[i]
  const nc = Math.max(cash, hold + p - fee)
  const nh = Math.max(hold, cash - p)
  cash = nc
  hold = nh
}
console.log(cash)
why: Buy at 1 and sell at 8 earns 7 - 2 = 5. Buy at 4 and sell at 9 earns 5 - 2 = 3. The total is 8.
Both new values are computed from the old ones (nc and nh), then assigned together.

think.q:
const prices = [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4], fee = 0
let cash = 0, hold = -prices[0]
for (let i = 1; i < prices.length; i++) {
  const p = prices[i]
  const nc = Math.max(cash, hold + p - fee)
  const nh = Math.max(hold, cash - p)
  cash = nc
  hold = nh
}
console.log(cash)
why: With no fee you can trade as often as you like: buy at 1, sell at 5 (profit 4), buy at 3, sell at 6 (profit 3). Total 7.
The same two states solve the whole family: just change the transitions.

think.q: Why is knowing only "the day" not enough for stock problems?
opts: The best next move depends on whether you currently hold a share, so that fact must be part of the state
why: On the same day, "holding" and "not holding" lead to different choices and different future profits.
Whenever the right move depends on a small piece of history (holding, cooldown, how many transactions are left), add it to the state.

think.q: The problem adds a cooldown: after selling, you cannot buy the next day. What do you change?
opts: Add a third state, "just sold / cooling down", with its own transitions
why: The cooldown is more history to remember, so it becomes a state. A state machine drawing (boxes and arrows between states) makes the transitions easy to read off.
Each new rule adds a state or an arrow, not a whole new algorithm.

think.q: What are the time and extra space of the two-variable solution for n days?
why: One pass, and only the previous values of the two states are kept.
Writing the full table first and then rolling it down to variables is a good way to get there.

try.task: Write maxProfitWithFee(prices, fee). You may buy and sell as many times as you like, but you can hold at most one share at a time, and you pay fee every time you sell. Return the largest total profit. An empty list gives 0.
try.hint: Keep cash = 0 and hold = -prices[0]. For each later price: newCash = max(cash, hold + price - fee), newHold = max(hold, cash - price). Return cash.

checks.t: one price and an empty list

checks.verify: const p = Array.from({ length: 200000 }, (_, i) => (i % 2 === 0 ? 1 : 10)); const t0 = Date.now(); const r = maxProfitWithFee(p, 2); assert(r === 100000 * 7 && Date.now() - t0 < 200, "wrong or too slow")

takeaway.key: When the best move depends on a small piece of history, keep one value per state (for example cash and hold) and update them together each step. O(n) time, O(1) space.
mistakes: Updating one state and then using the new value to update the other.
Forgetting the starting value of the hold state (-prices[0]).
Charging the fee on both buy and sell.
Returning hold instead of cash.

dryRun.title: Longest palindromic subsequence of "bbbab". dp[i][j] is the answer for the piece from i to j. Shorter pieces are solved first
dryRun.note: An interval DP solves small pieces first (by length), because a piece is built from the pieces inside it. The answer is the whole interval, dp[0][n-1]: 4 ("bbbb").

think.q:
function lps(s) {
  const n = s.length
  const dp = Array.from({ length: n }, () => new Array(n).fill(0))
  for (let i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    dp[i][i] = 1
    for (let j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
      dp[i][j] = s[i] === s[j] ? dp[i + 1][j - 1] + 2 : Math.max(dp[i + 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])
    }
  }
  return dp[0][n - 1]
}
console.log(lps("bbbab"))
why: The letters b, b, b, b (skipping the a) form the palindrome "bbbb" of length 4.
Here i goes from the end to the start so that dp[i + 1][...] is ready. That is another way to fill by growing length.

think.q: In interval DP, what does dp[i][j] usually mean?
opts: The answer for the first j items
The answer for the piece of the input from i to j, treated as its own problem
The distance between i and j
why: Both ends are part of the state, which is why the table is n × n. Only the cells with i <= j are used.
The transition looks at what happens at the ends, or at one split point inside the interval.

think.q: Why must shorter intervals be solved before longer ones?
opts: A long interval is built from smaller intervals inside it, which must be ready
why: dp[i][j] reads dp[i + 1][j - 1], dp[i + 1][j] and dp[i][j - 1], all of them shorter.
Two safe orders: by increasing length, or i from n - 1 down to 0 with j upwards.

think.q: For a string of length n, what is the time of this palindromic-subsequence DP?
why: There are about n² / 2 intervals and each is computed in O(1).
Interval DPs with a split point (matrix-chain multiplication, burst balloons) cost O(n³): n² intervals times n split points.

think.q: "Burst balloons": you pop balloons in some order and earn coins for each pop. The trick is to think about which balloon in an interval is popped last. Why does that help?
opts: When x is last, its neighbours inside the interval are fixed (the interval ends), so the two sides become independent smaller problems
It removes the need for a table
why: Choosing the last item to act on splits the interval into two parts that no longer affect each other.
This "choose the last one" move is the key idea of the harder interval DPs.

try.task: Write longestPalindromeSubseq(s). Return the length of the longest palindromic subsequence of s (letters in order, skipping allowed). An empty string gives 0.
try.hint: dp[i][j] for the piece from i to j. A single letter is 1. If s[i] === s[j] then dp[i+1][j-1] + 2, else the larger of dp[i+1][j] and dp[i][j-1]. Loop i downwards.

checks.t: one letter and an empty string

checks.verify: const t0 = Date.now(); assert(longestPalindromeSubseq("a".repeat(1500)) === 1500 && Date.now() - t0 < 1500, "wrong or too slow")

takeaway.key: Interval DP: dp[i][j] is the answer for the piece i..j, built from smaller pieces inside it. Fill by increasing length. Palindromic subsequence is O(n²); split-point problems are O(n³).
mistakes: Filling in an order where the smaller pieces are not ready.
Forgetting the single-letter base case.
Mixing up subsequence (can skip) and substring (continuous).
Using the wrong inside cell: it is [i + 1][j - 1] when the ends match.

dryRun.title: Shortest round trip through 3 cities from city 0. Distances: 0-1 is 10, 0-2 is 15, 1-2 is 20. A mask says which cities are visited (bit i = city i)
dryRun.note: When the state needs to remember a set of up to ~20 things, store the set as the bits of one integer. The state here is (which cities are visited, which one I am at).

think.q: console.log(1 << 3, 13 & (1 << 2), 13 | 2, 13 ^ 1)
why: 1 << 3 is 8 (a single bit). 13 is 1101 in binary, so 13 & 4 keeps bit 2 (value 4), 13 | 2 sets bit 1 (15), and 13 ^ 1 flips bit 0 (12).
The four moves you need: test a bit (&), set it (|), flip it (^), and make a mask (1 << i).

think.q:
const d = [[0, 10, 15], [10, 0, 20], [15, 20, 0]], n = 3, INF = Infinity
const dp = Array.from({ length: 1 << n }, () => Array(n).fill(INF))
dp[1][0] = 0
for (let mask = 1; mask < (1 << n); mask++)
  for (let last = 0; last < n; last++) {
    if (!(mask & (1 << last)) || dp[mask][last] === INF) continue
    for (let nx = 0; nx < n; nx++) {
      if (mask & (1 << nx)) continue
      const nm = mask | (1 << nx)
      dp[nm][nx] = Math.min(dp[nm][nx], dp[mask][last] + d[last][nx])
    }
  }
let best = INF
for (let last = 1; last < n; last++) best = Math.min(best, dp[(1 << n) - 1][last] + d[last][0])
console.log(best)
why: The table has 2ⁿ masks × n cities, and each cell tries n next cities: O(2ⁿ · n²).

think.q: How do you test whether bit i of mask is set (city i visited)?
why: Shift the bit down to position 0 and keep only that bit. mask & (1 << i) works too.
The other options mix numbers up with bit positions.

think.q: Why is bitmask DP used only when n is small, around 20 at most?
opts: The number of masks is 2ⁿ, which doubles with every extra item
why: 2²⁰ is about a million masks, and each has up to n × n transitions. 2³⁰ would be a billion masks, far too many.
Check the constraints: "n ≤ 15 or 20" is the signal for a bitmask solution.

think.q: What is the time of the bitmask solution to the travelling salesman problem?
why: It beats trying every order (n!) by remembering the best cost for each (set of visited cities, last city) pair.
For n = 20 that is about 400 million simple steps, the practical limit.

try.task: Write tsp(dist). dist[i][j] is the distance from city i to city j (a square matrix). Return the length of the shortest tour that starts at city 0, visits every other city exactly once and returns to city 0. With one city the answer is 0. It must handle up to 15 cities.
try.hint: dp[mask][last] = cheapest way to start at 0, visit exactly the cities in mask and stand at last. Start with dp[1][0] = 0. Finish with the best dp[full][last] + dist[last][0].

checks.t: a ring of 15 cities (neighbours cost 1, others 5)
checks.verify: const n = 15; const d = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => Array.from({ length: n }, (_, j) => (i === j ? 0 : (Math.abs(i - j) === 1 || Math.abs(i - j) === n - 1 ? 1 : 5)))); const t0 = Date.now(); assert(tsp(d) === 15 && Date.now() - t0 < 2000, "expected 15 in under 2 seconds")

takeaway.key: Bitmask DP stores a set as the bits of an integer. Test with (mask >> i) & 1, add with mask | (1 << i). Use it when n ≤ ~20. TSP: O(2ⁿ · n²) instead of O(n!).
mistakes: Using it with n in the hundreds.
Mixing up & (test) and | (set).
Forgetting to add the way back to the start.
Operator precedence: write mask & (1 << i) with brackets.

dryRun.title: Count the numbers from 1 to 45 that have no digit 4. N = 45, built digit by digit with a "tight" flag
rows: each choice is below the limit, so the next digit is free
no number starting with 4 is allowed
dryRun.note: Tight means "the digits so far are exactly the start of N", so the next digit is capped by the next digit of N. Once we go below N it becomes free (0 to 9). The state is only (position, tight), so we never loop up to N.

think.q:
function count(n) {
  const s = String(n)
  const memo = new Map()
  const go = (i, tight) => {
    if (i === s.length) return 1
    const key = i * 2 + (tight ? 1 : 0)
    if (memo.has(key)) return memo.get(key)
    const lim = tight ? +s[i] : 9
    let total = 0
    for (let d = 0; d <= lim; d++) {
      if (d === 4) continue
      total += go(i + 1, tight && d === lim)
    }
    memo.set(key, total)
    return total
  }
  return go(0, true) - 1
}
console.log(count(45))
why: The function counts the strings 00 to 45 without a 4, which is 36 (including 00), then - 1 removes the number 0. The answer is 35.
tight && d === lim stays true only while we copy N's digits exactly.

think.q:
function count(n) {
  const s = String(n)
  const memo = new Map()
  const go = (i, tight) => {
    if (i === s.length) return 1
    const key = i * 2 + (tight ? 1 : 0)
    if (memo.has(key)) return memo.get(key)
    const lim = tight ? +s[i] : 9
    let total = 0
    for (let d = 0; d <= lim; d++) {
      if (d === 4) continue
      total += go(i + 1, tight && d === lim)
    }
    memo.set(key, total)
    return total
  }
  return go(0, true) - 1
}
console.log(count(100))
why: From 00 to 99 there are 9 × 9 = 81 strings without a 4. Remove the number 0 to get 80 (the numbers 1 to 99), then add 100 itself, which has no 4. That is 81.
The code reaches the same answer without writing any of these cases by hand.

think.q: What does the tight flag mean?
opts: The digits chosen so far are exactly the leading digits of N, so the next digit may not go above N's next digit
why: If we already chose a smaller digit somewhere, the number is below N whatever follows, so later digits are free (0 to 9).
Forgetting this flag counts numbers bigger than N.

think.q: N can be as large as 10¹⁵. Why can you not simply loop from 1 to N and test each number?
opts: It would need a quadrillion steps, while digit DP needs about 15 positions × 2 states × 10 digits
The loop would give wrong answers
why: Digit DP works on the digits, not on the numbers: its cost grows with the number of digits (about log N).
This is the signal for digit DP: "count numbers up to N with a property of their digits", with N huge.

think.q: N has D digits. What is the time of the digit DP above?
why: There are D positions × 2 tight values, and each state tries up to 10 digits. That is about 20 × D steps.
If the property needs extra memory (like the sum of digits so far), that value joins the state and multiplies the size.

try.task: Write countWithout4(n). Return how many integers from 1 to n (included) do not contain the digit 4. n can be as large as 10**15.
try.hint: Turn n into a string of digits. go(i, tight) returns how many ways to fill positions i onwards. The limit is tight ? digit : 9. Skip the digit 4. Subtract 1 at the end for the number 0.

checks.verify: assert(countWithout4(4567) === 2915 && countWithout4(100000) === 59049, "does not match the brute-force count")

takeaway.key: Digit DP counts numbers up to N by their digits. State: (position, tight) plus whatever the property needs. Cost grows with the number of digits, not with N.
mistakes: Looping up to N when N is huge.
Forgetting the tight flag, or keeping it true after choosing a smaller digit.
Not removing the number 0 (or counting it by mistake).
Putting the memo key together wrongly so that tight and free states collide.

flags: knapsack: the "big" check uses a capacity that fits every item, so the expected value is just the sum of all values. It tests speed and the 1D loop, not selection. The selection tests are the first four checks.
dp-digit: brute-force expected counts for 4567 and 100000 and the answer for 10**15 (9**15) were computed in the generator.
dp-bitmask: the 15 city ring check expects 15 (neighbours cost 1).
The dry-run tables are traced by hand (concept dry runs are not machine-run).
